body: Scrape of a fork, side-on, against a roasting tin over the bin — a woman clearing up at a quarter past nine on a Tuesday in March. Her husband is upstairs answering one more email, which will take eleven minutes, as it has taken eleven minutes every night since January. She has a sentence ready. She has had it ready since Sunday and it is not an unkind one; it is about the way he says her mother’s name. She runs the tap and lets the tin fill, and by the time he comes down she has decided it will keep. On the shelf in the hall, next to the keys, is the folder from the marriage weekend they went on in October, with the ribbon still round it.
That Tuesday is the marriage. The weekend in October was not the marriage. It was a photograph of one, taken in unusually good light, and both of them meant every word of it at the time.

The dominant format for marriage teaching is the intensive: a weekend, a course, a retreat. Concentrated, expensive, emotionally significant and genuinely useful. Most couples come out of one with something named that had been unnameable for years.

It is worth taking the word conference literally. A conference is a place where people confer, and everything in the setting is arranged so that they can. Somebody else has the children. Somebody else is cooking. The phone is in a drawer, and both parties are, for once, not tired in the particular way they are tired at home. Under those conditions people say true things to each other, often for the first time in a year. The format is optimised for insight and it delivers insight reliably. What it cannot deliver is the conditions. Nobody gets to take the hotel home with them.

This band was built for the other end of that problem. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air now, running on ordinary evenings to ordinary kitchens rather than gathering anybody into a hall.

That is a more expensive way to work than it looks, and much harder to show anybody. A weekend can be photographed, ticketed and reported on. A station that is simply there at ten past seven on a Tuesday in March produces nothing to report, and it has to be paid for on every one of those evenings, including the empty ones. It is carried anyway, because those evenings are where marriages are actually decided. The intensive weekend has an excellent record on how people feel by Sunday night and almost none on where they are in March.

Church life has drifted towards the event for reasons that are practical rather than cynical. An event can be booked, sold, staffed, photographed and counted. It has a start, a finish and an outcome you can describe to somebody who was not there. The ordinary Tuesday has none of those properties. It cannot go on a poster, no one can be invited to it, and there is no way to tell afterwards whether it went well. So the calendar fills up with the things that can be measured, and the thing that actually carries a marriage is left to look after itself.

The dial is arranged the other way round. Every station holds one frequency permanently, no two share a number, and the schedule is published before it airs rather than assembled around whoever happens to be listening. Nothing is moved overnight to a better slot. That is not a technical detail; it is the precondition for a habit. A habit needs the world to hold still long enough for one to form, and almost nothing on a modern screen holds still for that long.
None of which is an argument against the weekend. It is an argument about what the weekend can be expected to do.

Because the thing that erodes a marriage was never a shortage of insight. It is the accumulated weight of ordinary Tuesdays: the tone used about a small thing, the conversation postponed for the fourth time, the assumption that hardened eighteen months ago and has not been checked since. Insight has a short half-life against that. Resolve formed on a Sunday night is usually gone by the middle of the following month, not because anybody was insincere but because resolve is not the mechanism that runs daily life. Habit is, and habit is built by low-intensity repetition, which is exactly what an intensive is not.
A marriage runs on Tuesdays, and nothing is scheduled for Tuesdays.

A man of about fifty gets in from work at twenty to seven. His wife is on lates and gets in at twenty past. Some time in the first winter of that arrangement he started putting a station on in the kitchen at about ten past, so that the house would have a sound in it when she opened the front door, because he had noticed that coming into a silent house at the end of a shift made her short with him for the first half hour and neither of them ever said so. He has never mentioned it. He would find it embarrassing to explain. Two years later the little speaker on the windowsill finally died, and she came in on the Thursday to a dark hall and stood there with her coat half off and said, not knowing quite why she was saying it, that something was wrong with the house.

That is the mechanism, and it is unimpressive by design. Nothing in it required a conversation, a workbook or a decision. It required somebody to do a small thing at ten past seven, on Tuesdays included, for two years.

It has to be said plainly that this is not treatment. A radio station cannot repair a marriage. If there is a real breach — a betrayal, an addiction, a contempt that has settled in and made itself at home — then music in the kitchen is not the answer and it would be dishonest to suggest otherwise. That needs a counsellor, or a confession, or exactly the kind of weekend this article has been putting in its place, with the phones in the drawer and somebody else minding the children.

But the low-intensity thing is not a rival to the intensive. It is the carrier. The weekend hands a couple a sentence they have needed for years; the ordinary evening is the only place that sentence will ever get said, and a house with something warm running in it at seven is easier to say a hard thing in than a silent one. Insight is a stock and it spends down. Habit is a flow. Anything you want to still be true in March has to be attached to the flow.

So the case is not that couples should stop going away for weekends. It is that a marriage is not carried by its exceptional hours, and treating the exceptional hours as the programme leaves the ordinary ones entirely unfurnished. Whatever is running in the room on a Tuesday is doing more work than anything said in a hall in October, because there are so many more Tuesdays and because nobody is braced for them.
All of which is theory until about ten past seven this evening. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, 40 frequencies carrying 29 languages between them. All of it runs to a schedule published in advance, so none of it is waiting to be asked what you are in the mood for, which matters on the evenings when neither of you is in the mood for anything.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. It is the covenant worship station, hosted by Elias Inspire, and it carries the SingItDone declaration albums: all twelve of the Inspire Family, one record each, singing who they already are before Yahuah rather than describing how the day went. The morning hour at six is the Morning Declaration and the evening hour at seven is called Sing What He Has Already Said, which is, as it happens, the exact grammar of a marriage. A vow is something you said once and then go on saying on the nights you do not feel it, until the saying carries the feeling back. That is the right thing to have running in a kitchen at ten past seven in March.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for on an ordinary Tuesday evening, which is how the next station gets built and how the ones already on air get better.

So do not book anything. Put HM 303.10 on tomorrow at about ten past seven, before whichever of you gets in last gets in, and then leave it alone and go and deal with the roasting tin. Do it again on Wednesday. Nothing will happen, and nothing is supposed to happen, and you will not be able to tell for months whether it is working. Then see where the two of you are in March. March is the only examination that has ever counted.
